Step 1 — Log In
Two steps. Takes under two minutes the first time.
1
Go to claude.ai and sign in with your School Tech work email
Use your @k12sta.com address — not a personal Gmail, not the Google sign-in button. If you haven't received an account invite yet, check your spam folder or contact Adam.
Common gotcha: If you see "Personal" instead of the School Tech workspace after logging in, you're in the wrong account. Log out and sign back in with your work email.
2
Find the Projects section in the left sidebar
AI tools are set up as individual Projects, each pre-configured for a specific job. Click the project name and start typing. No setup required — just open and ask.
Tip: The Projects list is on the left side of the screen. If you don't see it, make sure you're in the School Tech workspace (not a personal account).

Step 3 — Understand What You're Working With
Knowing what these tools are good at — and where to stay sharp — helps you get useful results faster.
It's good at
Drafting emails, responses, and customer-facing documents
Troubleshooting step by step
Explaining processes or policies in plain language
Turning rough notes into polished writing
Answering School Tech questions instantly
Keep in mind
Verify important facts before using them — especially specific dates, figures, or policy details
It doesn't remember previous conversations — each session starts fresh
Output is a strong first draft, not a final product — review before sending
Push back when it misses the mark — tell it specifically what's wrong and ask again
Step 4 — The One Rule That Has No Exceptions
Everything else in this guide is a tip. This is a hard requirement. When in doubt about any data, don't paste it — check the Restricted Data Reference Guide or ask Adam first.
Never paste student data
Student names, IDs, grades, attendance records, or anything from a Skyward student record. Even in a support case — describe the issue without including the data itself.
Never paste employee PII
Social Security numbers, payroll figures, HR records, performance data, or benefits information tied to a named individual. Anonymize first if you need help.
Never paste credentials
Passwords, API keys, authentication tokens, or login credentials of any kind — for any system, any account. Describe what you need instead.
Full department-by-department guidance is in the AI Restricted Data Reference Guide. Review it if you're ever unsure what's safe to include.
Step 5 — Your First Conversation
The fastest way to learn is to try something real. Here are a few first prompts that work well — pick one that fits your job.
Drafting support: "I need to respond to a customer who says their time clocks stopped syncing after last week's update. They're frustrated. Draft a calm response that acknowledges the issue and lets them know we're investigating."
Explaining a process: "Explain the process for helping a customer whose time clocks stopped syncing after a network change — what should I check first and how does the fix usually work?" (Use in STA Support Chat.)
Turning notes into something useful: "Here are my rough notes from a customer call: [paste notes]. Clean these up into a concise follow-up email I can send."
Exploring the AI program: "What AI tools are currently available to the support team, and what's coming next?" (Ask this in the AI Advisor project.)
If the first response isn't quite right: Don't start over. Stay in the same conversation and say exactly what's wrong — "too formal," "missing the part about X," "this is for a superintendent, not a teacher." It gets better fast when you're specific.
AI basics

New to working with AI? Start here. Ten quick concepts that make everything else make sense.

1. How to actually use AI chat

It's a conversation, not a search box. Don't type keywords, talk to it in full sentences: give it the task and the material, then refine with follow-ups like "make it shorter" or "you missed X."

STA example: instead of "customer refund angry," say "Draft a reply to this upset customer asking for a refund" and paste the actual email.

2. What an AI can and can't do

Strong at drafting, rewriting, summarizing, explaining, and brainstorming. Weak at exact facts, math, dates, and anything current, and it can sound confident while being wrong. Use it for the first draft, then you check the facts.

STA example: great for drafting a KB article; double-check any version numbers or specs it states.

3. What a prompt is

A prompt is just what you type to the AI, your request plus whatever it needs to do the job. Better prompts get better answers, which is what the Three-Ingredient Formula (what + context + format) is for.

STA example: "what" = draft a reply; "context" = the pasted email; "format" = under five sentences.

4. What is context

Context is everything the AI can see right now: your messages, anything you've pasted, and the project's setup files. It knows nothing outside that window. If it didn't see it, it doesn't know it.

STA example: pasting the actual time-clock error gets a far better answer than describing it from memory.

5. How AI memory works

A plain chat doesn't remember past conversations, each new chat starts blank. A Project keeps its setup files loaded every time, so the tool always knows STA basics, but it still won't recall what you typed yesterday unless it's saved in the project. That's why you re-paste the email or case each time.

STA example: Support Expert always knows the never-fabricate rule, but won't remember last week's ticket.

6. When to start a new chat vs keep going

Keep going while you're on the same task, the AI uses the whole conversation as context. Start a fresh chat when you switch topics, or when it gets confused and keeps repeating a mistake. A clean chat clears the clutter.

STA example: finished a customer reply and moving to a time-clock issue? Start a new chat.

7. Why it sometimes makes things up

When an AI doesn't know something, it can fill the gap with a confident-sounding guess, this is called a "hallucination." It's why every STA tool has the NEVER FABRICATE rule, and why you verify facts before sending.

STA example: if it cites a setting or price you can't confirm, treat it as a guess until you check.

8. How to give feedback or fix a bad answer

If an answer misses, just tell it what's wrong and it'll redo it: "that's too formal" or "wrong product name, it's X." You can also thumbs-down a response. Don't start over from scratch, correcting in place is faster and usually works.

STA example: "Good, but cut the apology paragraph and make it friendlier."

9. Project vs chat vs Cowork

A plain chat is a one-off conversation with no setup, fine for a quick personal question. A Project is a chat pre-loaded with STA instructions and reference files, so it already knows how we work, this is what you use daily (AI Advisor, Support Expert, the Salesforce Cohort). Cowork is the advanced desktop app that can work with files on your computer and run automations; it's limited to admins and power users.

STA example: ask a quick wording question in a plain chat, but do real support work in the Support Expert Project.

10. What Markdown (.md) files are

Markdown is plain text with light formatting, # for headings, dashes for bullets, **bold**, and it opens in any text editor with no special program. AI tools read and write it because it's clean and simple.

STA example: a Project's context/setup files are .md files, and some skills hand back .md output.

Common Questions
Do I need to explain what School Tech does every time I ask something?
No. Each project is already loaded with School Tech context — products, customers, processes, and tone. Just ask your actual question. If you're getting generic responses, it usually means the question is missing a specific detail (which customer, which product, what outcome you want), not that it needs more company background.
It remembered what I said earlier in the conversation but forgot it next time I opened it. Is that normal?
Yes. Within a single conversation, it remembers everything. When you close the conversation and start a new one, it starts fresh. This is by design. If you're building on previous work, paste the relevant context into the new conversation to pick up where you left off.
The response was wrong — what should I do?
Stay in the same conversation and tell it specifically what's wrong. "That's not right" is less useful than "the timeline you gave is wrong — this district is 3 months in, not new." The more specific you are about what missed, the better the next response will be. If a tool is consistently giving bad answers on a topic, let Adam know — tool instructions can be updated.
Can I use it for customer-facing writing?
Yes — that's one of the strongest use cases. Draft the response, review it, edit it to match your voice, then send. Don't send the raw output without reading it. You're responsible for everything that goes out under your name.
I have an idea for a tool that doesn't exist yet. Who do I tell?
Adam. Describe the workflow, who would use it, and what a useful result looks like. The AI program grows based on what the team actually needs, and new tools get built from those conversations.
